title: Regex basics in JavaScript
objectives: Read classes (`[^…]`, `\d \w \s`), quantifiers, anchors (`^ $ \b`), groups and alternation, and predict what a greedy vs a lazy quantifier matches
Choose the flag a job needs, telling `m` from `s` and knowing when text needs `u` (or `v`)
Pick `test`, `match`, `matchAll` or `replace` (with `$1` and `$<name>`), and predict what `match` and `replace` return with and without `g`
Explain and fix the `lastIndex` trap of a `g` regex reused with `test`
Escape user input with `RegExp.escape` (ES2025) before building a regex from it

sources.title: MDN: RegExp.prototype.test() — using test() with the global flag
TC39: Finished proposals (publication year of each feature)

questions.prompt: Which pattern accepts `"12345"` but rejects both `"123456"` and `"zip 12345"`?
questions.explanation: Only both anchors pin the whole input. `/\d{5}/` is satisfied by five digits anywhere — `"123456"` contains `"12345"`. `/^\d{5}/` checks only the start, so `"123456"` passes; `/[0-9]{5}$/` checks only the end, so `"zip 12345"` and `"123456"` both pass. (`[0-9]` and `\d` are the same class.)

options.text: Anything that starts with `cat` or ends with `dog` — `catalog` and `hotdog` included

questions.explanation: `|` has the lowest precedence, so the pattern is `(^cat)` or `(dog$)`, and each anchor applies to its own side only. To mean "exactly cat or dog", group the alternation: `/^(?:cat|dog)$/`. "Contains" would need no anchors at all — `"a cat"` fails here, because `^cat` wants `cat` at the start.

`.` doesn't match line terminators unless the `s` (`dotAll`) flag is set. `m` is the usual wrong guess: it changes what `^` and `$` match (each line's start and end), not what `.` matches. `g` only changes how many matches are found, and `u` changes how characters are counted, not whether `.` accepts a newline.

questions.prompt: `/^.$/.test("😀")` returns `false`. Why, and what makes it `true`?

options.text: Without `u` (or `v`) the regex sees the emoji as two UTF-16 code units, so `.` matches only half — add `u`
`.` skips special characters like emoji unless the `s` flag is set
Emoji have no case, so the `i` flag is needed

questions.explanation: `"😀".length` is 2: outside Unicode mode a regex works on UTF-16 code units, and this emoji is a surrogate pair. `u` (or `v`) makes the regex work on code points, so `.` takes the whole character. `[\s\S]` has the same problem as `.` — it matches one code unit — and `s` only adds line terminators to what `.` accepts. Any pattern that runs on human text, with `.`, quantifiers or `\p{…}`, wants `u` or `v`.

questions.prompt: From `"a=1&b=two&c=3"` you need every pair, each with its `key` and `value` groups. Which call gives you that?
questions.explanation: `matchAll` yields one full match object per hit, each with its `groups` and `index`. `match` with `g` returns only the matched strings — `["a=1", "b=two", "c=3"]` — and without `g` only the first match. `matchAll` requires the `g` flag; without it, it throws a `TypeError`.

questions.prompt: With `s = "2026-10-17"` and `p = /(?<y>\d{4})-(?<m>\d{2})-(?<d>\d{2})/`, which calls produce `"17/10/2026"`? Select all that work.
questions.explanation: `$<name>` inserts a named group, and named groups are numbered too, so `$3/$2/$1` works as well. A template literal is evaluated *before* `replace` is called, so `${d}` looks up a JavaScript variable named `d` — a `ReferenceError` here. `$d` isn't a replacement pattern at all, so it's inserted literally and the result is `"$d/$m/$y"`.

questions.prompt: A module has `const SLUG = /^[a-z0-9-]+$/g;` and `export const isSlug = (s) => SLUG.test(s);`. `isSlug("post-1")` returns `true`, then `isSlug("post-2")` returns `false`. Why?

options.text: With `g`, `test` resumes at `SLUG.lastIndex` (6 after the first match), where `^` can't match — drop the `g`
A regex literal caches its first result — build the regex inside the function
`^` and `$` match only once per regex unless the `m` flag is set
`test` needs the `y` flag to start from index 0

questions.explanation: The first `test` succeeds and leaves `SLUG.lastIndex` at 6. The second call searches `"post-2"` from index 6, where `^` can never match, so it fails — and resets `lastIndex` to 0, so a third call would succeed. Nothing is cached: building the regex inside the function hides the bug only because each call then starts with a fresh `lastIndex`. `m` is about line breaks, and `y` makes things stricter, not better: a sticky regex must match exactly at `lastIndex`.

questions.prompt: A search box runs `new RegExp(query, "i")` on whatever the user typed. Someone searches for `c++`. What happens, and what's the fix?

options.text: It throws `SyntaxError: … Nothing to repeat`; build the pattern from `RegExp.escape(query)` (ES2025)
It matches the text `c++`; nothing to fix
It matches `c` followed by anything; adding the `u` flag makes the input literal
It throws; pass the query through `encodeURIComponent` first

questions.explanation: The query is parsed as a pattern, and the second `+` has nothing to repeat, so the constructor throws. `RegExp.escape("c++")` returns `\x63\+\+` (the leading letter is escaped too), which matches the text literally. `encodeURIComponent` escapes for URLs, not regexes: it turns `+` into `%2B`, which never matches `c++`. The `u` flag makes the parser stricter, not literal. On runtimes older than Node 24, Chrome 136, Firefox 134 or Safari 18.2, use a `RegExp.escape` polyfill.

snippets.question: What do the three lines print?
snippets.explanation: With `g`, the first `test` matches and sets `re.lastIndex` to 1. The second call searches `"a"` from index 1, finds nothing, returns `false` and resets `lastIndex` to 0, so the third call matches again. The regex carries state between calls — even across different strings. Without the `g`, every call prints `true`.

snippets.question: What do the two lines print?
snippets.explanation: `.+` is greedy: it runs to the end of the string, then backs off only until a `>` can match — the *last* `>`. `.+?` is lazy: it stops at the first `>` that lets the match finish. `/<[^>]+>/` gets `<b>` without relying on laziness, because the class can't cross a `>`.

snippets.question: What do the three lines print?
snippets.explanation: A string pattern is replaced once, and so is a regex without `g`: only the `g` flag makes `replace` change every match. For a plain string, `"a-b-c".replaceAll("-", "+")` is the readable alternative.

snippets.question: What does the last line print?
snippets.explanation: Without `g`, `match` returns the first match *with* its groups, so `one[1]` is the first capture group: `"2026"`. With `g`, it returns only the matched strings — `["2026-", "10-"]` — so `all[1]` is the second whole match, and the groups are gone. Use `matchAll` when you need every match and its groups.
